title: Code of Good Practice for Milk Producers in the dairy industry

lessons.title: Purpose and scope of the Code of Good Practice
lessons.html:
Why a code of practice

Consumers, retailers and processors expect milk that is safe, of consistent quality and produced responsibly. The South African dairy industry, through its organisations such as Milk SA and the Milk Producers' Organisation, has developed a Code of Good Practice for milk producers. It translates legal requirements and good dairy farming principles into practical standards on the farm. It is closely aligned with international guidance such as the FAO and IDF Guide to Good Dairy Farming Practice. Always work from the current version issued by the industry and any buyer-specific requirements.

What the Code aims to achieve

  • Milk that is safe for consumers and free from residues and contaminants.
  • Healthy animals managed with good welfare.
  • Hygienic milking and milk handling.
  • Responsible feed and water use.
  • Protection of the environment.
  • Fair and safe treatment of workers.
  • Records that demonstrate compliance and allow traceability.

Relationship to the law

The Code does not replace legislation. It helps producers meet laws such as the Foodstuffs, Cosmetics and Disinfectants Act 54 of 1972 and its hygiene regulations for milking sheds and milk, the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984, Act 36 of 1947 for stock remedies and feeds, the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962, the National Water Act 36 of 1998, the OHS Act 85 of 1993 and labour laws. Many milk buyers require producers to follow the Code or equivalent standards and audit them against it.

The supervisor's role

Owners commit to the Code, but supervisors make it happen every day. You train staff in procedures, check that they are followed, keep records, and report gaps to the manager. During audits or inspections by buyers, the Dairy Standard Agency or health officials, your records and the state of the parlour, dairy and animals are the evidence.

Self-assessment

Use the Code's checklists to assess the farm regularly, not only before an audit. Record findings, agree corrective actions with the manager and follow them up.

lessons.title: Applying the Code on the farm
lessons.html:
Key areas and practices

AreaPractical requirements
Animal healthHerd health plan with the vet; controlled disease testing and vaccination such as brucellosis and TB; identification of all animals; quarantine of new animals
MedicinesUse registered remedies as label or vet prescription directs; record every treatment; mark treated cows; observe milk and meat withdrawal periods; store medicines securely
Milking hygieneClean, dry teats before milking; milkers with clean clothing and gloves; correct milking routine; post-dipping; maintained milking machine
Milk handlingRapid cooling and temperature records; clean milk room protected from pests; cleaned and sanitised equipment
Feed and waterFeed from reliable suppliers; safe storage; no mouldy or contaminated feed; clean water always available
Animal welfareFreedom from hunger and thirst, discomfort, pain and disease, fear and distress; ability to express normal behaviour; calm handling; humane euthanasia when needed
EnvironmentManagement of effluent and manure to protect water; safe disposal of chemicals, containers and carcasses
PeopleTraining, safe work, protective equipment, fair labour practices

The five freedoms

Animal welfare in the Code reflects the internationally used five freedoms listed above. On a dairy this means adequate feed and water, comfortable lying areas and shade, prompt treatment of lameness and mastitis, no rough handling, dogs or electric prodders used carelessly, and appropriate social groups.

Records that demonstrate compliance

  • Animal identification and movement register.
  • Treatment and medicine purchase records.
  • Vaccination and disease testing certificates.
  • Milk tank temperature and cleaning records.
  • Feed delivery and storage records.
  • Staff training records.
  • Effluent management and water records.

When something goes wrong

If antibiotic milk reaches the tank, a cooling failure occurs or a cow is mistreated, act immediately: stop collection of contaminated milk, inform the manager and buyer as the procedure requires, record what happened, find the cause and retrain or change procedures.

Key points

  • The Code turns legal and buyer requirements into practical farm standards.
  • It covers animal health, medicines, milking hygiene, milk handling, feed, welfare, environment and people.
  • Treated cows must be marked and withdrawal periods observed.
  • Records are the evidence of compliance in audits.
  • Self-assess regularly and correct gaps promptly.
